languages.name: Tatar
languages.label: left
languages.where: Tatarstan and the wider Volga-Ural region of Russia
languages.about: A Kipchak Turkic language and, with Russian, an official language of the Republic of Tatarstan. Its closest relative is Bashkir, spoken just to the east.

languages.name: Bashkir
languages.label: right
languages.where: Bashkortostan, in the southern Ural mountains of Russia
languages.about: A Kipchak Turkic language, official in the Republic of Bashkortostan. It is so close to Tatar that speakers of the two can largely follow each other.

languages.name: Fang
languages.label: left
languages.where: Equatorial Guinea, northern Gabon and southern Cameroon
languages.about: A tonal Bantu language and the most widely spoken language of mainland Equatorial Guinea. With Ewondo it belongs to the Beti-Fang group.

languages.name: Ewondo
languages.label: right
languages.where: Central Cameroon, around the capital Yaoundé
languages.speakers_est: Roughly half a million native speakers, and many more who use it as a second language
languages.about: A tonal Bantu language of the Beti-Fang group, closely related to Fang. It is widely used as a common language in and around Yaoundé.

languages.name: Torwali
languages.label: left
languages.where: The upper Swat valley, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
languages.about: A Dardic language of the mountains of northern Pakistan, considered endangered. Local community groups have built schools and learning materials in Torwali, and its Common Voice recordings are among the few that exist.

languages.name: Hazaragi
languages.label: left
languages.where: Central Afghanistan (Hazarajat), with communities in Quetta, Pakistan and in Iran
languages.speakers_est: A few million; estimates vary widely
languages.about: A variety of Persian (Dari) spoken by the Hazara people. It has its own pronunciation and vocabulary, including words borrowed from Turkic and Mongolic languages. Common Voice lists it as "Hazargi".

languages.name: Urdu
languages.label: bottom
languages.where: Pakistan, where it is the national language, and India
languages.speakers_est: About 70 million native speakers and over 200 million in total
languages.about: A major Indo-Aryan language, very close to Hindi in everyday speech and written in a Perso-Arabic script. As the dominant language of the region, it is often the base that voice tools for smaller Pakistani languages are built on.

languages.name: Kohistani Shina
languages.label: right
languages.where: The Indus valley in Kohistan, northern Pakistan
languages.speakers_est: Estimates are uncertain; likely a few hundred thousand
languages.about: A Dardic language of the Shina group, a neighbour of Torwali in the mountains of northern Pakistan. We use it in place of Kashmiri, its better-known Dardic relative, which has no dataset on Mozilla Data Collective yet.

languages.name: Rioplatense Spanish
languages.label: right
languages.where: The Río de la Plata region, Argentina and Uruguay (Buenos Aires, Montevideo)
languages.about: The Spanish of Argentina and Uruguay, known for "vos" in place of "tú" and a "sh"-like sound for ll and y. Its melody is often said to sound Italian, a legacy of large-scale Italian immigration.

languages.name: Scottish English
languages.label: left
languages.about: English as spoken in Scotland, with its own vowels and rhythm. English is the language most voice technology is built for first, so it is a useful reference point on the map.
